2.text: I spoke with a man named Kaˊtɪk, who declared that he did not want to

3.text: live any longer. He gave as his reason, that fortune was adverse to him,

4.text: that all his relatives had died, and that he was afraid that his herd at some

5.text: time might begin to dwindle away, although at the time of speaking his

6.text: reindeer were prospering. I did not pay much attention to his words, but the

7.text: next winter I heard that he really had ordered himself to be strangled.

8.text: At the head waters of the river Omolon I met a family four of whose

9.text: members had taken their own lives within four years without any apparent

10.text: reason. Their neighbors felt much afraid, and expressed the opinion that the

11.text: spirits who wanted more prey had treacherously led them on to self-destruction.

12.text: A rough kind of compassion for all suffering characterizes the Chukchee

13.text: mind. Once in my presence a Reindeer man rescued a ptarmigan that was

14.text: being hunted down by a hawk and had come to the camp exhausted, and

15.text: angrily expostulated with some children who wanted to catch the bird. Another

16.text: time a Reindeer woman paid a ransom to one of my dog-drivers to stop him

17.text: from punishing one of his own dogs.

18.text: Still more remarkable is the generosity which the Reindeer Chukchee

19.text: display toward everybody who is in need, even if he be of strange tribe and

20.text: language. On the Chaun tundra live a small number of Lamut families,

21.text: members of various clans who have wandered northward. They are a peculiar

22.text: people, very poor and very indolent; and fully one-half of their food is drawn,

23.text: with very little pay, from the herds of their well-to-do Chukchee neighbors.

24.text: Similar relations have existed of late between the Chukchee and the

25.text: Tungus on the western Kolyma. At present, however, most of those Chuk-

26.text: chee are poor; and the few rich breeders farther to the west have acquired

27.text: a taste for trade, and have gradually adopted the ways of the Yakut or

28.text: Russian dealers. In occasional times of need the starving Russian settlements

29.text: on the Kolyma and Anadyr were relieved, up to a very recent time, by the

30.text: neighboring reindeer-breeders, who often slaughtered several hundred animals,

31.text: taking very little or no pay for them. This disposition to help the needy

32.text: of a strange tribe probably sprang from the peculiar relations of both branches

33.text: of the Chukchee, which in so many respects form a unit, although they differ

35.text: The woman, as is the case among all peoples, is more compassionate

36.text: than the man. In the tale of “Elendi and his Sons,” quoted before, the hero

37.text: reproves the wife of his foe, who had been very severe to his neighbors,

38.text: saying, “Why did you not feed your neighbors in secret? Why did you not

39.text: give them food yourself?”¹ In reality, in the camps of rich reindeer-breeders,
